items.stem: A weight lifter lifts a barbell as shown in the figure. List two forces that are acting on the barbell. Are these forces balanced if the weight lifter keeps the barbell steady?
items.answer: The two primary forces acting on the barbell are the downward gravitational force exerted by the Earth and the upward force applied by the weightlifter’s hands. Yes, if the weightlifter keeps the barbell completely steady, these two opposing forces are equal in magnitude and are balanced.

items.stem: Two players R and S are participating in an arm-wrestling match as shown in the figure. At the instant, when the arms tilt to the front direction (out of the page towards you), are the forces exerted by the players balanced? If not, which player exerted the larger force?
items.answer: No, the forces are not balanced because the arms are moving and accelerating in a specific direction. The player who is applying their force in the direction of the tilt (out of the page towards you) has exerted the larger force.

items.stem: An object is moving with a constant velocity. Is there a net force acting upon it?
items.answer: No, there is no net force acting upon it. According to Newton’s first law of motion, an object maintains a constant velocity only when the net external force acting on it is zero.

items.stem: Suppose, no net force is acting on an object. Which of the following situations are possible? (i) Object remains at rest if at rest. (ii) Object keeps moving with a constant velocity if already moving. (iii) Object is moving with a constant acceleration.
items.answer: Only situations (i) and (ii) are possible when no net force is acting on an object. Situation (iii) is not possible because having a constant acceleration requires a continuous, non-zero net force.

items.stem: In the real world, it is difficult to find a situation where no forces are acting on an object. But by applying additional forces, a condition can be achieved where the net force on the object is zero. Explain with the help of an example.
items.answer: In everyday life, forces like friction and gravity are always present and acting on objects. However, we can create a zero net force situation by applying an external force that exactly balances these opposing forces. For example, if you push a heavy box across the floor at a constant speed, the forward pushing force you apply is exactly equal to the backward force of friction. Because these forces cancel each other out, the net force is zero and the box does not accelerate.

items.stem: A toy car of mass 100 g is moving with a constant velocity of 0.5 m s-1. What is the net force acting on the toy car?
items.answer: The net force acting on the toy car is zero. Because the car is moving with a constant velocity, its acceleration is zero, which implies that all forces acting on it are perfectly balanced.

items.stem: Two children of different masses are sitting on identical swings. To impart identical initial acceleration, for which child would you require to apply a larger force? Explain why.
items.answer: You would require a larger force to accelerate the child with the greater mass. According to Newton’s second law of motion, force is equal to mass multiplied by acceleration. Therefore, to achieve the exact same acceleration, a heavier object inherently requires a proportionally larger applied net force.

items.stem: How are glass items packed for transportation using a bubble wrap or hay protected from damage?
items.answer: Materials like bubble wrap or hay are highly compressible and act as soft cushions for fragile items. During a sudden stop or collision, these materials increase the time duration over which the glass item comes to rest. By increasing the time of the impact, the rate of change of momentum is decreased, which results in a much smaller force being exerted on the glass, thereby preventing it from breaking.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: Why does a fire person sometimes struggle when holding the pipe issuing water?
items.answer: A fire person struggles because of the equal and opposite reaction principle described by Newton’s third law of motion. The hose pipe exerts a large forward force to push a massive amount of water out at high speeds. Simultaneously, the rushing water exerts an equally large backward reaction force on the pipe, causing a strong recoil that the fireperson must constantly fight to hold steady.

items.stem: Suppose a spacecraft is moving in a region of space where the gravitational force acting upon it is negligible. Suggest how can it change its velocity.
items.answer: To change its velocity in the absence of external forces like gravity, the spacecraft must use its own thrusters or engines. By expelling exhaust gases backward at a high speed, the spacecraft exerts a strong force on the gases. According to Newton’s third law, the gases exert an equal and opposite forward reaction force on the spacecraft, providing the net force needed to accelerate and alter its velocity.

items.stem: Using a horizontal force F, a table is moved across the floor at a constant velocity. How much is the frictional force exerted by the floor on the table?
items.answer: Since the table is moving at a constant velocity, the net force acting on it is zero. Therefore, the frictional force exerted by the floor on the table must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the applied horizontal force F.

items.stem: For a ball moving on a smooth frictionless surface, choose the appropriate option that will make the following statements physically correct. (i) If no net force is applied on the ball, the velocity of the ball will remain the same/increase/decrease. (ii) If a net force is applied on the ball in the direction of its motion, the magnitude of the velocity of the ball will remain the same/increase/decrease. (iii) If a net force is applied on the ball in a direction opposite to the direction of its motion, the magnitude of the velocity of the ball will remain the same/increase/decrease.
items.answer: (i) remain the same. According to Newton’s first law of motion, an object in motion will continue to move with a constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force. (ii) increase. A net force applied in the direction of motion provides an acceleration in the same direction, causing the velocity to increase. (iii) decrease. A net force applied opposite to the motion causes deceleration, which reduces the magnitude of the ball’s velocity.

items.stem: Two blocks P and Q on a smooth horizontal surface are shown in Figure (a) and Figure (b). Two forces of magnitudes 4 N and 5 N are acting in opposite directions on block P, while block Q is moving with a constant velocity. Which of the following statement is correct?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: (iii) Both P and Q experience a net force.

options.label: D
options.text: (iv) Neither P nor Q experiences a net force.

items.answer: Option (i) is correct. Block P experiences unbalanced forces (5 N right and 4 N left), resulting in a net force of 1 N. Block Q is moving with constant velocity, which implies its acceleration is zero, so it experiences zero net force according to Newton’s first law.

items.stem: While practising for the snake boat race (Vallum kalli in Kerala), 100 oarsmen are rowing a boat together. Out of these, 95 row backwards to propel the boat forward. But by mistake, 5 oarsmen row in the opposite direction. If each oarsman applies a horizontal force of 200 N, what is the net force on the snake boat? (Ignore drag forces, air friction, etc.)
items.answer: The 95 oarsmen rowing backwards propel the boat forward with a total force = 95 × 200 N = 19,000 N. The 5 mistaken oarsmen row forwards, pushing the boat backwards with a total force = 5 × 200 N = 1,000 N. The net force acting on the snake boat = 19,000 N - 1,000 N = 18,000 N in the forward direction.

items.stem: When a net force acts on an object, we observe that the object accelerates:

items.answer: Option (iv) is correct. According to Newton’s second law of motion, the acceleration of an object is in the direction of the net force and its magnitude is directly proportional to the net force applied.

items.stem: A sailor jumps out from a small boat to the shore (Fig). As the sailor jumps forward, will the boat move? If yes, in which direction and why.
items.answer: Yes, the boat will move backward, away from the shore. According to Newton’s third law of motion, as the sailor pushes the boat backward with their feet to jump forward, the boat exerts an equal and opposite force forward on the sailor. This backward force applied by the sailor causes the boat to move in the reverse direction.

items.stem: During a high jump event, a landing mat or sand bed is placed for the athlete to fall upon (Figure). Explain the reason behind it.
items.answer: The landing mat or sand bed provides a soft, compressible surface that increases the time it takes for the falling athlete to come to a complete stop. According to Newton’s second law of motion, force is equal to the rate of change of momentum. By extending the stopping time, the rate of change of momentum decreases, which significantly reduces the impact force exerted on the athlete’s body, thereby preventing serious injuries.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: A hand cart loaded with vegetables collides with an identical but empty hand cart. During the collision:

options.label: A
options.text: (i) the loaded cart exerts a force of larger magnitude on the empty cart.

options.label: B
options.text: (ii) the empty cart exerts a force of larger magnitude on the loaded cart.

options.label: C
options.text: (iii) neither cart exerts a force on the other.

options.label: D
options.text: (iv) the loaded cart and the empty cart, both exert an equal magnitude of force on each other.

items.answer: Option (iv) is correct. Newton’s third law of motion states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction; hence, regardless of their different masses, both carts exert an equal magnitude of force on each other during the collision.

items.stem: The acceleration-mass graph for the acceleration produced by a force on objects of different masses is plotted in the figure. The curve passes through the points (1 kg, 10 m/s²), (2 kg, 5 m/s²) and (4 kg, 2.5 m/s²). Plot the force-mass graph for this case.
items.answer: From the given graph, as the mass increases the acceleration decreases, an inverse relationship. Reading the key points off the curve and multiplying mass by acceleration: for 1 kg and 10 m/s² the force is 10 N; for 2 kg and 5 m/s² the force is 10 N; for 4 kg and 2.5 m/s² the force is again 10 N. The product of mass and acceleration is the same at every point, so the applied force is constant at 10 N. The force-mass graph is therefore a straight horizontal line parallel to the mass axis, drawn at the 10 N level.

items.stem: The velocity-time graph of an object of mass 10 kg moving along a straight line is shown in the figure. The graph is a straight line rising from 10 m/s at the start to 30 m/s at 8 s. Calculate the force acting on the object by using the graph.
items.answer: From the given graph the initial velocity is 10 m/s at the start and the final velocity is 30 m/s at 8 s. The acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken, that is (30 m/s - 10 m/s) divided by 8 s, which is 20/8 or 2.5 m/s². Using Newton’s second law, force is mass multiplied by acceleration, so the force is 10 kg times 2.5 m/s². The force acting on the object is 25 N.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 50 g moving with a speed of 100 m/s enters a heavy stationary wooden block and stops after penetrating a distance of 50 cm. Estimate the stopping force acting on the bullet (assume that the bullet undergoes constant acceleration within the block).
items.answer: Given: mass of the bullet is 50 g, that is 0.05 kg; initial velocity is 100 m/s; final velocity is 0 m/s since it stops; distance is 50 cm, that is 0.5 m. Using the kinematic equation in which the square of the final velocity minus the square of the initial velocity equals twice the acceleration times the distance: 0 minus 10000 equals 2 times the acceleration times 0.5 m, so the acceleration is -10000 m/s². By Newton’s second law the force is mass multiplied by acceleration, 0.05 kg times -10000 m/s², which is -500 N. The stopping force acting on the bullet is 500 N, directed opposite to its motion.

items.stem: An ace footballer converted a penalty shot by kicking the football with a speed of 108 km h-1. The estimated force they imparted was 800 N. The mass of the football was 0.4 kg. Calculate the time of contact between their foot and the ball.
items.answer: Final velocity (v) = 108 km/h = 108 × (5/18) m/s = 30 m/s. Assuming the ball started from rest, initial velocity (u) = 0 m/s. Force (F) = 800 N. Mass (m) = 0.4 kg. Using Newton’s second law to find acceleration (a): F = ma, so a = F/m = 800/0.4 = 2000 m/s². Now, using the equation v = u + at, we get 30 = 0 + 2000 × t, t = 30/2000 = 0.015 s. The time of contact between the foot and the ball is 0.015 seconds.

items.stem: An object of mass 2 kg moving with a constant velocity of 10 m s-1 encounters a rough patch where the force of friction on the object is 7 N. At the same time, an additional constant force of 3 N opposing the motion is applied on the object. After entering the rough patch, how much distance does the object travel before coming to rest?
items.answer: Given: mass m = 2 kg; initial velocity u = 10 m s-1; final velocity v = 0 m s-1, since it comes to rest; force of friction f = 7 N opposing the motion; additional opposing force F = 3 N, also opposing the motion. Both forces act opposite to the direction of motion, so they add up: Fnet = -(f + F) = -(7 + 3) = -10 N. Using Newton’s second law, the acceleration is a = Fnet/m = -10/2 = -5 m s-2, a deceleration. Using the equation of motion v² = u² + 2as, the distance is s = (v² - u²)/(2a) = (0 - 100)/(2 × -5) = -100/-10 = 10 m. The object travels 10 m before coming to rest.

items.stem: A tractor pulls a harrow (a ploughing tool) of mass m1 with a net force F resulting in an acceleration of a1. The same tractor pulls a trolley of mass m2 with a force F producing an acceleration of a2. If the tractor now pulls the trolley with the harrow placed on it (with the same force F), then obtain an expression for the resulting acceleration in terms of a1 and a2. Ignore friction.
items.answer: From Newton’s second law, for the harrow: m1 = F/a1. For the trolley: m2 = F/a2. When they are pulled together, the combined mass is m = m1 + m2. Substituting the values of m1 and m2: m = (F/a1) + (F/a2) = F(1/a1 + 1/a2) = F[(a1 + a2)/(a1 × a2)]. The resulting acceleration (a) when force F is applied to this combined mass is: a = F/m; a = F/{F[(a1 + a2)/(a1 × a2)]}. The F cancels out, leaving: a = (a1 × a2)/(a1 + a2).

items.stem: When the pole of a bar magnet is brought close to a magnetic compass, the bar magnet and the compass needle (which is also a magnet) exert a magnetic force on each other. As per Newton’s third law of motion, both the forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. However, the compass needle moves, whereas the bar magnet does not move. Explain why.
items.answer: Even though the forces acting on both the bar magnet and the compass needle are equal in magnitude, their effects are very different due to their masses. According to Newton’s second law, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (a = F/m). The compass needle has a very tiny mass, so the magnetic force causes a large, noticeable acceleration. In contrast, the bar magnet is significantly heavier, so the same magnitude of force produces an acceleration that is too small to be noticed, and often not enough to overcome the force of static friction holding it in place.

items.stem: Which of the following physical quantities is required to completely specify a force acting on an object?
items.answer: Force is a physical quantity that requires both magnitude and direction for its complete description. If either the magnitude or the direction of the applied force changes, the overall effect on the object also changes. Therefore, force is classified as a vector quantity, unlike scalar quantities which only have magnitude and no specific direction associated with them.

items.stem: What is the standard SI unit of force as established in scientific measurement?
items.answer: The standard international unit of force used in physics is the newton, which is symbolised by a capital letter N. This unit is named after the scientist Sir Isaac Newton. The magnitude of force applied on an object expresses its overall strength and determines the resulting acceleration produced in the object according to the second law.

items.stem: Consider a scenario where two teams are playing a game of tug of war. If both teams pull the rope in opposite directions with equal force, what will be the state of the rope?
items.answer: In a game of tug of war, when both teams pull the rope with equal force in opposite directions, the net force acting on the rope becomes exactly zero. These equal and opposite forces are called balanced forces. Because the forces are perfectly balanced, the rope does not move and remains in its initial state of rest.

items.stem: Two forces of 15 N and 10 N act on a wooden block resting on a table. If both forces are applied in the exact same direction, what is the magnitude of the net force acting on the block?
items.answer: When two or more forces are applied simultaneously on an object in the same direction, their individual magnitudes add up to provide the total effective force. In this specific case, adding the applied force of fifteen newtons and ten newtons yields a combined net force of twenty-five newtons acting in the direction of the initial application.

items.stem: Determine the magnitude and the direction of the net force acting on the block shown in the diagram.
items.answer: The forces act in opposite directions along the same line. The net force is the difference between their individual magnitudes, which calculates to exactly four newtons. The direction of the resultant net force is fundamentally determined by the larger applied force, which clearly points towards the right side of the block.

items.answer: When two unbalanced forces act on an object in completely opposite directions, the net force is determined by calculating the difference between their respective magnitudes. Here, twenty minus twelve equals eight newtons. This resulting net force always acts in the direction of the larger applied force, causing the object to accelerate in that specific direction.

2. It can change the direction of motion of an object.
3. It can change the shape of an object.
Which of the above statements are correct?
items.answer: An applied external force has the physical capability to alter the state of motion of a body from rest, change its velocity or direction while moving, and even deform its structural shape. Examples include kicking a stationary ball, hitting a moving cricket ball with a bat, and squeezing a lemon, demonstrating all these fundamental physical effects clearly.

items.stem: When you push a heavy wooden box placed on a rough horizontal floor, it does not move immediately. Which specific force acts in the direction opposite to your push to prevent the motion?
items.answer: The force of friction is a contact force that always arises between two surfaces trying to slide past one another. It consistently acts in a direction completely opposite to the direction of the applied force or intended motion. The box remains stationary until the applied pushing force eventually exceeds this opposing maximum static frictional force.

items.stem: In a classroom activity, a stack of coins is pulled with a rubber band across different horizontal surfaces. On which of the following surfaces will the stack of coins travel the greatest distance before coming to rest?
items.answer: The magnitude of frictional force fundamentally depends heavily upon the relative smoothness or roughness of the interacting surfaces. A highly polished marble floor offers the least possible resistance among the given options. Consequently, the opposing frictional force is minimised, allowing the moving stack of coins to travel a significantly larger distance before gradually coming to rest.

items.stem: Who among the following historical scientists first argued through a series of thought experiments that if all impediments to motion are removed, a body moving along a horizontal plane will continue to move indefinitely?
items.answer: In the seventeenth century, Galileo Galilei radically proposed through extensive thought experiments that objects in motion do not naturally require a continuous applied force to keep moving. He argued that if opposing forces like friction were completely eliminated, a body moving on a perfectly horizontal plane would persist in its uniform motion indefinitely without ever stopping.

items.answer: The first law of motion formally describes inertia, which is the natural tendency of physical objects to stubbornly resist any change in their current state of rest or uniform motion. items.answer: By pulling the hands backward, the fielder effectively increases the time duration over which the high velocity of the ball reduces to zero. This fundamental relationship is universally expressed by the simple algebraic formula F = ma, indicating that applied force is directly proportional to the acceleration produced in the mass.

items.stem: Who first proposed the idea that objects tend to resist changes in their state of motion?
items.answer: Isaac Newton used the word inertia to describe this tendency of objects, building upon the earlier thought experiments conducted by scientist Galileo Galilei.

items.stem: State Newton’s first law of motion.
items.answer: An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues with constant velocity, unless a net force acts upon the object.

items.stem: What is the relationship between the net force acting on a body and its acceleration according to the first law?
items.answer: If the net force acting on an object is strictly zero, the body cannot change its velocity, meaning its resulting acceleration is exactly zero.

items.stem: What would happen to the position-time graph of an object moving with constant velocity?
items.answer: When an object is moving with a constant velocity and zero net force, its position-time graph will always be represented as a straight line.

items.stem: Write the mathematical expression for Newton’s second law of motion.
items.answer: Newton’s second law of motion is mathematically expressed by the equation F = ma, where F is force, m is mass, and a is acceleration.

items.stem: What is the scientific term for the product of an object’s mass and its velocity?
items.answer: The product of an object’s mass and its velocity is known as its momentum, which helps explain Newton’s second law in more comprehensive terms.

items.stem: How does pulling hands backward while catching a fast cricket ball help the fielder?
items.answer: Pulling hands backward increases the time duration for stopping the ball, reducing its acceleration and thereby minimizing the required stopping force and potential injury.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: Give one real-life application where extending collision time is used for safety in vehicles.
items.answer: Airbags in vehicles quickly inflate during a collision to cushion the passenger, increasing the stopping time and greatly reducing the force exerted on them.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: Define one newton of force based on Newton’s second law.
items.answer: One newton is defined as the exact amount of force that produces an acceleration of one meter per second squared on a one-kilogram mass.

items.stem: What is the approximate value of acceleration due to gravitational force by the Earth near its surface?
items.answer: The acceleration due to Earth’s gravitational force is denoted by g, and its fairly constant value near the surface is 9.8 meters per second squared.

items.stem: State Newton’s third law of motion.
items.answer: Whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal and completely opposite force on the first object.

items.stem: State one major difference between the action and reaction forces described in Newton’s third law.
items.answer: Although action and reaction forces are always equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, they specifically act on two completely different interacting objects simultaneously.

items.stem: Why do we sometimes struggle to walk on wet polished floors or ice?
items.answer: We struggle to walk on these surfaces because the drastically reduced force of friction makes it difficult to push the ground backward effectively without slipping.
items.concept: Friction depends on surfaces in contact

items.stem: Give one reason why a fired bullet and the recoiling gun do not have the same acceleration despite equal forces.
items.answer: Although the interacting forces are strictly equal in magnitude, the resulting accelerations differ significantly because the gun’s mass is much larger than the bullet’s mass.

items.stem: How does a rocket utilize Newton’s third law to launch into space?
items.answer: The rocket engine forcefully expels exhaust gases downwards, simultaneously exerting an equal and opposite upward reaction force on the rocket, allowing it to lift off.

items.stem: Give one example of Newton’s third law in daily life involving water.
items.answer: When a canoeist forcefully pushes water backwards with a paddle, the water simultaneously pushes the paddle and canoe forward with an equal and opposite force.

items.stem: What is meant by treating connected boxes as a “single system” in physics?
items.answer: Treating connected boxes as a single system means analyzing their combined motion together, requiring consideration of only external forces while completely ignoring their internal forces.
items.concept: Connected objects as a single system

items.stem: State one similarity in how Newton’s second law applies to a single object versus a system of connected objects.
items.answer: In both scenarios, the total resulting acceleration of the entity is directly proportional to the net external force and inversely proportional to the total mass.

items.stem: What is the significance of distinguishing between internal and external forces in a multiobject system?
items.answer: Distinguishing them greatly simplifies scientific analysis because internal forces simply balance each other out, meaning only the external forces dictate the entire system’s overall acceleration.

items.stem: Under what condition does an object floating on water remain perfectly stationary?
items.answer: An object floating on water remains stationary when the downward gravitational force is perfectly balanced by the equal and opposite upward buoyant force of water.

items.stem: What is the relationship between the applied force and acceleration for an object of fixed mass?
items.answer: For an object of fixed mass, the acceleration produced is directly proportional to the net force applied to it, acting in the same exact direction.

items.stem: Explain the concept of balanced forces with the help of an example. What happens to the state of motion of an object when balanced forces act on it?
items.answer: Balanced forces occur when multiple forces acting on an object are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. In this situation, the forces effectively cancel each other out, resulting in a net force of exactly zero. Because the net force is zero, balanced forces do not change the state of rest or the state of uniform motion of the object. For example, in a tug-of-war, if both teams pull the rope with equal force from opposite sides, the rope remains completely stationary.

items.stem: Draw the position-time and velocity-time graphs for an object moving with a constant velocity. What does this indicate about the net force acting on the object?
items.answer: When an object moves with a constant velocity, its speed and direction do not change. According to Newton’s first law of motion, an object maintains a constant velocity only when the net external force acting on it is exactly zero. The position-time graph is a straight sloping line, and the velocity-time graph is a flat horizontal line, both visually confirming that no unbalanced force is causing acceleration or deceleration to the object.

items.stem: What is the SI unit of force? How can you use a simple spring balance to measure the magnitude of a force?
items.answer: The SI unit of force is the newton, represented by the symbol N. A spring balance contains a coiled spring inside it that stretches when a force is applied. To measure the magnitude of a pulling force, you simply attach the object or apply the pull to the free hook at the end of the spring balance. The spring stretches in proportion to the applied force, and the reading indicated on the calibrated scale provides an approximate measure of the force’s magnitude.

items.stem: Study the scenario shown in the diagram, in which two people push a stalled car in the same direction. How do you calculate the magnitude and direction of the net force in this scenario? How would this change if they pushed the car from opposite ends?
items.answer: In this scenario, since both people are applying forces on the stalled car in the exact same direction, the magnitude of the net force is calculated by simply adding the magnitudes of their individual forces together. The direction of this net force will be in the same forward direction. If they were to push the car from opposite ends, the forces would oppose each other. The net force would then be the difference between their magnitudes, acting in the direction of the larger applied force.

items.stem: State Newton’s second law of motion. How does this mathematical relationship help us formally define one newton of force?
items.answer: Newton’s second law of motion states that when a net force acts on an object, it accelerates in the direction of the net force. The magnitude of acceleration is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass. Mathematically, it is expressed as force equals mass times acceleration. Using this law, one newton of force is formally defined as the exact amount of force required to produce an acceleration of one meter per second squared on an object having a mass of one kilogram.

items.stem: State Newton’s first law of motion. Explain how this law contradicts the ancient misconception regarding moving objects.
items.answer: Newton’s first law of motion states that an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move with a constant velocity, unless a net external force acts upon it. For centuries, people mistakenly believed that a continuous applied force was absolutely necessary to keep an object moving at a steady speed. Galileo and Newton corrected this by showing that in the absence of opposing forces like friction, a moving object will continue its motion indefinitely without any additional force.

items.stem: A student claims that a heavy box pushed across a room requires a constant continuous force just to keep it moving at a constant velocity, which proves Newton’s first law wrong. Do you agree? Justify.
items.answer: I disagree with the student’s conclusion. The situation does not prove Newton’s first law wrong; rather, it involves the presence of friction. When moving a heavy box, the floor exerts a frictional force in the direction opposite to the motion. To keep the box moving at a constant velocity, you must apply a continuous forward force that exactly equals the opposing frictional force. This balances the forces, making the net force zero, which perfectly aligns with Newton’s first law of motion.

items.stem: What is inertia? Which famous scientist introduced this term to describe the inherent tendency of objects regarding motion?
items.answer: Inertia is the inherent physical property or tendency of objects to resist any change in their current state of rest or state of uniform motion. If an object is resting, it tends to stay resting; if it is moving, it tends to keep moving steadily. The famous scientist Isaac Newton used this specific word and concept to frame his first law of motion in 1687, building upon earlier revolutionary thought experiments conducted by Galileo Galilei in the seventeenth century regarding frictionless movement.

items.stem: When you try to push a heavy box resting on the floor with a small force, it does not move. Explain the scientific reason behind this observation.
items.answer: When you apply a small force to a stationary heavy box, it does not move because an opposing force called friction arises between the bottom surface of the box and the floor. This frictional force acts in the exact opposite direction to your applied push. As long as your applied force is smaller than or equal to the maximum opposing friction, the two forces balance each other out perfectly. Since the net force remains zero, the box does not accelerate and stays at rest.

items.stem: Draw a diagram of a block placed at rest on a horizontal table, showing the vertical forces acting on it. Why does the block not move vertically despite these forces?
items.answer: The block experiences a downward gravitational force exerted by the Earth and an upward normal force exerted by the surface of the table. The block does not move in the vertical direction because these two specific forces are exactly equal in magnitude and strictly opposite in direction. They completely cancel each other out, resulting in a net vertical force of zero. According to Newton’s first law, with zero net force, the block remains stationary vertically.

items.stem: How is the acceleration of an object mathematically related to its applied force? What happens to the acceleration if the object’s mass is doubled while the applied force remains constant?
items.answer: According to Newton’s second law of motion, the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net applied force and inversely proportional to the object’s mass. This means that a larger net force produces a proportionally larger acceleration. However, because acceleration is inversely related to mass, if you double the mass of the object while keeping the applied force exactly the same, the acceleration will decrease by half. Heavier objects require much more force to achieve the same acceleration as lighter ones.

items.stem: Explain the physics behind why a cricketer gradually pulls their hands backward while catching a fast-moving ball.
items.answer: When catching a fast-moving cricket ball, the fielder gradually pulls their hands backward to intentionally increase the time duration over which the ball’s high velocity is reduced to zero. According to Newton’s second law of motion, an increase in the time taken to stop the ball significantly reduces the magnitude of the deceleration. Consequently, a much smaller opposing force is required to bring the ball to rest, which safely minimizes the impact force on the fielder’s hands and prevents serious injuries.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: When an apple falls towards the Earth, Newton’s third law states the Earth also experiences an equal upward force. Why is the Earth’s acceleration towards the apple not noticeable?
items.answer: It is true that the apple and the Earth exert equal and opposite gravitational forces on each other. However, according to Newton’s second law of motion, the acceleration produced by a force is inversely proportional to the mass of the object. While the apple has a tiny mass and accelerates at 9.8 m/s², the Earth has an incredibly massive size. When this same small force is divided by the gigantic mass of the Earth, the resulting acceleration is infinitesimally small and impossible to notice.

items.stem: Compare balanced and unbalanced forces with respect to their magnitude, direction, and their ultimate effect on the state of motion of an object.
items.answer: Balanced forces are two or more forces acting on an object that are exactly equal in magnitude but strictly opposite in direction. Because they cancel each other completely, their net force is zero, meaning they do not change the object’s state of rest or constant velocity. In contrast, unbalanced forces are unequal in magnitude or do not act in perfectly opposite directions. They produce a non-zero net force, which inevitably causes the object to accelerate, change its speed, or alter its direction.

items.stem: Study the given diagram of a weightlifter holding a 30 kg barbell perfectly steady above her head. What force does the Earth exert on the barbell, what upward force must the weightlifter apply, and what is the net force acting on the barbell?
items.answer: The Earth exerts a downward gravitational force on the barbell, which is calculated by multiplying its mass by the acceleration due to gravity. For a 30 kg mass, this force is 30 kg × 9.8 m/s², equalling 294 N downwards. To keep the barbell perfectly steady, the weightlifter must apply an upward force that exactly balances this weight. Therefore, she applies a force of 294 N upwards. Because these opposing forces are balanced, the total net force acting on the barbell is zero.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 0.1 kg is fired horizontally from a 5 kg gun. If the force acting on the bullet is 2 N, calculate the initial accelerations of both the bullet and the gun.
items.answer: Given: mass of bullet, m₁ = 0.1 kg; mass of gun, m₂ = 5 kg; force acting on the bullet, F = 2 N. By Newton’s second law of motion: a = F/m. Acceleration of the bullet: a₁ = F/m₁ = 2 N ÷ 0.1 kg = 20 m/s² (forward). By Newton’s third law of motion, the bullet exerts an equal and opposite reaction force of 2 N on the gun in the backward direction. Acceleration of the gun: a₂ = F/m₂ = 2 N ÷ 5 kg = 0.4 m/s² (backward). According to Newton’s third law of motion, the force propelling the bullet forward and the recoil force pushing the gun backward are equal and opposite, both measuring 2 N. Using Newton’s second law, acceleration equals force divided by mass. The gun’s initial acceleration is calculated as 2 N divided by 5 kg, yielding 0.4 m/s². The bullet’s initial acceleration is 2 N divided by 0.1 kg, which results in a significantly much higher acceleration of 20 m/s² due to its tiny mass.

items.stem: What is the essential function of airbags in modern vehicles? How do they prevent serious injuries during a sudden collision?
items.answer: Airbags are designed to act as soft, compressible cushions that rapidly inflate inside a vehicle during a severe collision. Without an airbag, a passenger would hit the hard dashboard, stopping almost instantly. The airbag significantly increases the time duration over which the passenger’s forward velocity is reduced to zero. According to Newton’s second law of motion, increasing this stopping time drastically reduces the deceleration, which in turn reduces the magnitude of the force exerted on the person’s body, preventing serious trauma.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: A student pushes a stationary 25 kg block on a horizontal floor. The maximum force of friction opposing the motion is 50 N. Calculate the acceleration of the block if the student applies a constant force of 55 N forward.
items.answer: When the student pushes the block with a forward force of 55 N, the rough floor exerts a maximum opposing frictional force of 50 N backward. The net force acting on the block is the difference between these two opposing forces, which is 55 N minus 50 N, giving a net forward force of 5 N. According to Newton’s second law, acceleration is net force divided by mass. Dividing the 5 N net force by the 25 kg mass gives an acceleration of 0.2 m/s².

items.stem: Renu argues that since action and reaction forces are always exactly equal and opposite, they should cancel each other out, meaning no object should ever be able to accelerate. Do you agree? Justify.
items.answer: I strongly disagree with Renu’s reasoning. While Newton’s third law states that action and reaction forces are indeed equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, the crucial detail is that they always act on two distinctly different objects. Forces can only cancel each other out if they are acting on the exact same object. Because the action acts on one body and the reaction acts on the other interacting body, they do not balance each other, and both objects can independently accelerate.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram showing a balloon sliding along a stretched thread. Explain the forces causing the balloon’s motion based on Newton’s laws.
items.answer: When the neck of the inflated balloon is released, the stretched rubber forcefully expels the trapped air molecules out in the backward direction. According to Newton’s third law of motion, this action causes an equal and opposite reaction force. The expelled air pushes back on the balloon material with the same magnitude of force in the forward direction. Since this forward reaction force is unbalanced, it provides acceleration, causing the balloon to swiftly move forward along the guiding thread.

items.stem: Compare the resulting acceleration of a highly massive truck and a small light car if both are pushed on a smooth road with the identical net force. Which law of motion primarily explains this relationship?
items.answer: If an identical net force is applied to a massive truck and a light car, the light car will experience a significantly larger acceleration compared to the heavy truck. This inverse relationship is entirely explained by Newton’s second law of motion, which explicitly states that the acceleration produced by a net force is inversely proportional to the mass of the object. Since the truck has much greater mass, it possesses more inertia and stubbornly resists changes to its motion, resulting in smaller acceleration.

items.stem: Study the diagram showing two blocks on a smooth surface. Block P has a 5 N force acting on it to the right and a 4 N force acting on it to the left, while block Q moves at a constant velocity with no external horizontal force shown. Which block is currently experiencing a net force? Describe the expected state of motion for both blocks based on the given forces.
items.answer: Block P is experiencing a net force because the opposing horizontal forces acting on it are unequal. The net force on block P is 1 N to the right (5 N minus 4 N), meaning block P will continuously accelerate in the rightward direction according to Newton’s second law. Block Q, moving at a constant velocity on a frictionless surface without any external arrows shown, has a net force of zero. According to Newton’s first law, it will continue moving uniformly forever.

items.stem: State Newton’s third law of motion. Explain how a person is able to row a canoe forward through a lake using a paddle.
items.answer: Newton’s third law of motion states that whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite force back on the first object. When rowing a canoe, the paddler uses the paddle to push the water forcefully in the backward direction. In response to this action, the water pushes the paddle—and consequently the canoe attached to it—forward with an equal reactive force, enabling the canoe to accelerate smoothly across the lake.

items.stem: Why is it notoriously difficult to walk safely on wet polished floors or smoothly frozen ice? Explain using the concept of interacting forces.
items.answer: Walking fundamentally relies on the friction between your footwear and the ground surface. When you walk, your foot pushes backward against the ground, and by Newton’s third law, the frictional force from the ground pushes you forward. Wet polished floors or smooth ice have remarkably low levels of surface friction. Without sufficient grip, your foot slips backward when trying to push, and the ground cannot provide an adequate forward reaction force, making it extremely difficult to propel yourself safely forward.
items.concept: Friction depends on surfaces in contact

items.stem: Draw a block diagram showing a system of two boxes connected by a string being pulled to the right. Why is the tension force in the connecting string considered an internal force when analysing the whole system?
items.answer: When treating both boxes and the string collectively as a single unified system, the tension forces exist entirely inside the boundaries of this chosen system. According to Newton’s third law, Box 1 pulls Box 2 rightward with tension T, and Box 2 pulls Box 1 leftward with an equal tension T. Because these action-reaction pairs act strictly within the system’s boundary, they perfectly cancel each other out when calculating the overall net force, thus making them internal forces.

items.stem: What are the two vertical forces acting on a plastic ball floating motionless on the surface of a pond? Why does the ball remain completely at rest vertically?
items.answer: When a plastic ball is floating motionless on water, it is subjected to two distinct vertical forces. The first is the gravitational force exerted by the Earth, which pulls the ball downwards. The second is the buoyant force exerted by the liquid water, which pushes the ball upwards. The ball remains completely at rest in the vertical direction because these two forces are perfectly equal in magnitude and directly opposite in direction, creating balanced forces and a net vertical force of zero.

items.stem: Draw a velocity-time graph for a car starting from rest and moving with uniform acceleration. How can you use this graph alongside Newton’s laws to find the net force acting on the car?
items.answer: The velocity-time graph for a uniformly accelerating car is a straight line inclined to the time axis. To find the net force acting on the car, you first calculate the physical slope of this straight line. The value of this slope directly gives the constant acceleration of the car. Once the acceleration is determined, you multiply it by the known mass of the car using Newton’s second law equation (F = ma) to calculate the exact net force acting upon it.

items.stem: When dealing with two attached objects like a cart towing a trailer, why do physicists often treat them as a single combined system? How does this mathematically simplify finding the acceleration?
items.answer: Physicists often treat connected objects as a single combined system to greatly simplify motion analysis. When viewed as one system, the complex internal forces acting between the individual objects—such as the tension in the towing rope—cancel each other out completely in pairs. This allows us to use Newton’s second law by simply dividing the total external pulling force by the combined total mass of both objects, effortlessly yielding the system’s overall acceleration without needing to solve multiple simultaneous equations.
items.concept: Connected objects as a single system

items.stem: Have you ever noticed people cracking a fresh hard coconut in one go by hitting it forcefully on the ground? Explain the science behind how the shell breaks using Newton’s laws.
items.answer: Breaking a hard coconut in one go is a practical application of Newton’s second law of motion. When the fast-moving coconut violently hits the hard, unyielding ground, its velocity is abruptly reduced to absolute zero in a fraction of a second. Because the time duration of this impact is extremely short, the resulting deceleration is massively high. Consequently, the ground exerts an enormous reaction force back on the coconut shell, which surpasses its structural strength, causing it to instantly crack open.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: Imagine a hypothetical scenario where the force of friction completely disappears from the entire world. Describe two immediate severe consequences this would have on everyday human movement or transportation.
items.answer: If friction were to completely vanish from the world, the consequences would be catastrophic for daily activities. First, humans would be entirely unable to walk or run; without friction to provide a forward reaction force against our footsteps, we would simply slip uncontrollably in place. Second, wheeled vehicles like cars and bicycles could neither steer, accelerate, nor apply brakes safely. Any moving object on a flat path would simply glide forever at a constant speed, unable to deliberately stop or change direction.

items.stem: (a) Draw a diagram showing the horizontal and vertical forces acting on a wooden block being pushed across a table but remaining completely stationary? (b) Identify the balanced force pairs? (c) Explain how Newton’s first law of motion applies to this specific situation?
items.answer: (a) The diagram shows four forces acting on the block: its weight, the gravitational pull of the Earth, acting vertically downwards; the normal reaction of the table acting vertically upwards; the applied push acting horizontally forwards; and the force of friction acting horizontally backwards. The two vertical arrows are equal in length and opposite in direction, and so are the two horizontal arrows. (b) When a wooden block is pushed but remains stationary, multiple forces act upon it, but they form balanced pairs. The downward gravitational force exerted by the Earth is perfectly balanced by the upward normal force exerted by the table’s surface. Similarly, the applied horizontal push is completely balanced by an equal and opposite force of friction acting between the bottom of the block and the table. Since the opposing forces cancel each other out, the net force acting on the block is zero. (c) According to Newton’s first law of motion, an object at rest will remain at rest unless acted upon by a non-zero net force. Because the forces are balanced, the state of the block does not change, and it continues to remain completely stationary on the table without experiencing any acceleration.

items.stem: (a) What is the force of friction and what generally causes it? (b) Describe briefly how you would use a spring balance and a wooden block to show that friction depends on the nature of the surfaces in contact? (c) Why do we need to continuously apply a forward force to keep a bicycle moving at a constant velocity?
items.answer: (a) The force of friction is a resistive force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact. It arises due to the interactions and interlocking between the surfaces at the microscopic level. (b) To demonstrate that friction depends on the nature of the surfaces, place a wooden block on a normal table and pull it with a horizontally attached spring balance until it just starts moving. Note the reading, which indicates the force of friction. Repeat this experiment by placing the same block on different surfaces like polished marble or a laminated top. The varying spring balance readings will clearly indicate that rougher surfaces offer significantly greater friction than smoother ones. (c) Although Newton’s first law states objects move uniformly without external forces, we must continuously apply a pedal force to keep a bicycle moving to perfectly counter this ever-present friction and maintain a zero net force.
items.concept: Friction depends on surfaces in contact

items.stem: (a) Draw a velocity-time graph showing the motion of a fast cricket ball being caught in two scenarios: an abrupt catch and a gradual catch where the fielder pulls their hands backwards? (b) Explain the scientific principle behind pulling the hands back using Newton’s second law? (c) How do vehicle airbags use this same principle during collisions?
items.answer: (a) On the velocity-time graph the velocity of the ball falls from its high initial value to zero in both catches. For the abrupt catch the line drops almost vertically over a very brief interval, so its slope, the deceleration, is very steep. For the gradual catch, in which the fielder pulls the hands back, the same fall in velocity is spread over a much longer time, so the line slopes gently and the deceleration is far smaller. (b) According to Newton’s second law of motion, the acceleration of an object is inversely proportional to the time taken for a change in velocity. When a cricketer catches a fast-moving ball and pulls their hands backwards, they strategically increase the time duration over which the high velocity of the ball reduces to zero. This extended time significantly decreases the deceleration of the ball. Consequently, a much smaller net force is required to stop the ball, thereby minimising the impact and preventing serious injury to the fielder’s hands. (c) This identical scientific principle is applied in vehicle air-bags. During an abrupt collision, an air-bag inflates to provide a soft compressible cushion. It delays the passenger’s forward motion, increasing the time over which their velocity reaches zero. This critically reduces the acceleration and lowers the exerted force, substantially reducing the risk of fatal injuries.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: (a) State Newton’s second law of motion and express it mathematically? (b) A sports car of mass 1200 kg accelerates uniformly from rest to a velocity of 20 m/s in 4 seconds. Calculate the acceleration of the car and the net force acting on it?
items.answer: (a) Newton’s second law of motion states that when a net force acts on an object, it accelerates in the direction of the net force, where the magnitude of acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the object’s mass. Mathematically, it is expressed as a = F/m, which is commonly rearranged as F = ma, where F is the net force, m is the mass, and a is the acceleration. (b) For the sports car, the initial velocity is zero, and the final velocity is twenty metres per second over a time interval of four seconds. Using the kinematic equation, acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time, yielding five metres per second squared. Using the second law equation, the net force is the mass of twelve hundred kilograms multiplied by the acceleration of five, giving a net force of six thousand newtons.

items.stem: (a) State Newton’s third law of motion? (b) Explain in detail how this law enables a person to walk naturally on the ground? (c) If the action and reaction forces are always equal and opposite, why do they not simply cancel each other out when we walk?
items.answer: (a) Newton’s third law of motion states that whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object is simultaneously exerting an equal and opposite force on the first object. (b) This fundamental principle perfectly explains the mechanics of human walking. When you attempt to walk forward, your foot actively pushes against the ground in the backward direction. In immediate response, the ground applies an equal and opposite reaction force on your foot in the forward direction. It is this forward frictional force from the ground that actually propels your body ahead. (c) Although the action and reaction forces are completely equal in magnitude and strictly opposite in direction, they do not cancel each other out because they act on entirely different objects. One force forcefully acts on the ground while the opposite reaction force acts on your body, allowing net movement to successfully occur.

items.stem: (a) According to gravitational principles, the Earth and a falling apple exert equal and opposite forces on each other. Why does the apple fall towards the Earth, but the Earth does not visibly move towards the apple? (b) A 0.05 kg bullet is fired from a 4 kg gun with a force of 10 N; calculate the initial acceleration of both the bullet and the gun?
items.answer: (a) According to Newton’s third law, the Earth and a falling apple exert equal and opposite gravitational forces on each other. However, Newton’s second law dictates that acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. The mass of the Earth is astronomically larger compared to the tiny mass of the apple. Consequently, the same magnitude of force produces a significant, observable acceleration in the light apple, causing it to fall rapidly, but an infinitesimally small, unnoticeable acceleration in the massive Earth. (b) For the numerical portion, we use the formula acceleration equals force divided by mass. The initial acceleration of the bullet is calculated by dividing the ten newton force by its mass of zero point zero five kilograms, resulting in two hundred metres per second squared. The gun’s recoil acceleration is ten newtons divided by its four kilogram mass, yielding exactly two point five metres per second squared.

items.stem: (a) Draw the position-time and velocity-time graphs for an object moving along a straight line with a constant velocity? (b) Based on Newton’s first law, what is the net force acting on this object? (c) Explain why a moving object eventually comes to rest in the real world if no continuous forward push is applied?
items.answer: (a) The position-time graph is a straight line sloping uniformly upwards from the origin, and its constant slope gives the constant velocity of the object. The velocity-time graph is a horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis, showing that the velocity does not change with time and that the slope, which is the acceleration, is zero. (b) Based on Newton’s first law of motion, an object moving with a constant velocity has a strictly zero net force acting upon it. Because there is absolutely no change in either the speed or the direction of the object, its acceleration is zero, which mathematically confirms the complete absence of a net external force. In a theoretical frictionless environment, such an object would continue moving indefinitely. (c) However, in the real world, an object moving across a surface eventually comes to rest because forces are rarely completely absent. Even if no human pushes it, the unseen force of friction between the interacting surfaces, alongside air resistance, continuously acts in the direction directly opposite to the object’s motion. This unbalanced opposing force creates negative acceleration, gradually slowing the object down until it finally stops moving completely.

items.stem: (a) Using the relationships established in Newton’s second law, how does the acceleration of an object change when the applied net force is exactly doubled while its mass remains constant? (b) How does the acceleration change if the mass is doubled while the force remains constant? (c) Calculate the specific force required to impart an acceleration of 2.5 m/s² to a block of mass 10 kg?
items.answer: (a) According to Newton’s second law of motion, the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting upon it and inversely proportional to its mass. Therefore, if the applied net force is intentionally doubled while the mass is kept entirely constant, the resulting acceleration of the object will also be exactly doubled. (b) Conversely, if the mass of the object is doubled while applying the exact same constant force, the object inherently becomes heavier and much harder to move, causing the resulting acceleration to be strictly reduced to exactly half of its original value. (c) To calculate the urgently required force for the specific block, we apply the foundational mathematical equation Force equals mass multiplied by acceleration. By multiplying the block’s given mass of ten kilograms by the desired acceleration of two point five metres per second squared, we conclusively determine that a net force of twenty-five newtons is required.

items.stem: (a) Describe the general mechanism of a rocket launch into space using the principles of Newton’s third law of motion? (b) How did the Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 use this exact same physical principle to intentionally slow down and achieve a successful soft landing near the Moon’s south pole?
items.answer: (a) A rocket launch is a classic and powerful demonstration of Newton’s third law of motion, which states that every action has an equal and opposite reaction acting on different bodies. During a launch, the rocket engine rapidly burns fuel to produce continuously expanding exhaust gases. The engine forcefully expels these highly pressurised gases downwards towards the ground. This deliberate downward push constitutes the action force. Simultaneously, the expelled exhaust gases exert an exactly equal and opposite reaction force upwards on the rocket itself. Because this upward thrust is significantly larger than the gravitational weight of the rocket, it smoothly accelerates upwards into space. (b) The Vikram lander ingeniously utilised this exact principle but in reverse for its lunar descent. By actively firing its thrusters in the downward direction of its motion, the expelled gases created a strong opposing upward reaction force. This counter-force deliberately reduced the lander’s velocity, enabling a completely safe soft landing.

items.stem: A truck starts from rest and rolls down a hill with a constant acceleration. It travels a distance of 400 m in 20 s. Find its acceleration. Find the force acting on it if its mass is 7 tonnes (Hint : 1 tonne = 1000 kg).
items.answer: Given, initial velocity, u = 0 m s-1; distance, s = 400 m; time, t = 20 s; mass, m = 7 metric tons = 7000 kg. By the second equation of motion, s = ut + ½at², so 400 m = (0 m s-1 × 20 s) + (½ × a × (20 s)²), that is, 400 m = ½ × a × 400 s². Hence, a = 800 m / 400 s² = 2 m s-2. By Newton’s second law of motion, F = m × a = 7000 kg × 2 m s-2 = 14000 N.

items.stem: A stone of 1 kg is thrown with a velocity of 20 m s-1 across the frozen surface of a lake and comes to rest after travelling a distance of 50 m. What is the force of friction between the stone and the ice?
items.answer: Given, mass, m = 1 kg; initial velocity, u = 20 m s-1; final velocity, v = 0 m s-1; distance, s = 50 m. By the third equation of motion, v² - u² = 2as, so (0 m s-1)² - (20 m s-1)² = 2 × a × 50 m, that is, -400 m²s-2 = 100 m × a. Hence, a = -400 m²s-2 / 100 m = -4 m s-2. By Newton’s second law of motion, F = m × a = 1 kg × (-4 m s-2) = -4 N. The force of friction between the stone and the ice is 4 N, acting opposite to the motion of the stone.
items.concept: Friction brings moving objects to rest

items.stem: A 8000 kg engine pulls a train of 5 wagons, each of 2000 kg, along a horizontal track. If the engine exerts a force of 40000 N and the track offers a friction force of 5000 N, then calculate : (a) the net accelerating force, (b) the acceleration of the train, and (c) the force of wagon 1 on wagon 2.
items.answer: Given, mass of the engine, m1 = 8000 kg; mass of each wagon, m2 = 2000 kg; number of wagons, n = 5. Total mass of the 5 wagons = 2000 kg × 5 = 10000 kg. Force exerted by the engine, F1 = 40,000 N. Frictional force offered by the track, F2 = 5000 N. (a) Net accelerating force, F = F1 - F2 = (40,000 - 5,000) N = 35,000 N. (b) Acceleration of the train, a = F/m = 35000 N / 10000 kg = 3.5 m s-2. (c) Force of wagon 1 on wagon 2 = (35,000 - 35,000/5) N = (35,000 - 7000) N = 28,000 N.
items.concept: Connected objects as a single system

items.stem: An automobile vehicle has a mass of 1500 kg. What must be the force between the vehicle and road if the vehicle is to be stopped with a negative acceleration of 1.7 m s-2?
items.answer: Given, mass of the vehicle, m = 1500 kg; acceleration, a = -1.7 m s-2. By the second law of motion, F = m × a = 1500 × (-1.7) = -2550 N. The negative sign shows that the force is in a direction opposite to the direction of motion of the vehicle.

items.stem: A hockey ball of mass 200 g travelling at 10 m s-1 is struck by a hockey stick so as to return it along its original path with a velocity at 5 m s-1. Calculate the change of momentum occurred in the motion of the hockey ball by the force applied by the hockey stick.
items.answer: Given, mass of the hockey ball, m = 200 g = 200/1000 = 0.2 kg; initial velocity of the ball, u = 10 m s-1; final velocity of the ball, v = -5 m s-1 (the hockey ball travels in the opposite direction). Initial momentum of the ball = m × u = 0.2 kg × 10 m s-1 = 2 kg m s-1. Final momentum of the ball = m × v = 0.2 kg × (-5 m s-1) = -1 kg m s-1. Change of momentum = mv - mu = (-1 - 2) kg m s-1 = -3 kg m s-1.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 10 g travelling horizontally with a velocity of 150 m s-1 strikes a stationary wooden block and comes to rest in 0.03 s. Calculate the distance of penetration of the bullet into the block. Also calculate the magnitude of the force exerted by the wooden block on the bullet.
items.answer: Given, mass, m = 10 g = 10/1000 kg = 0.01 kg; initial velocity, u = 150 m s-1; final velocity, v = 0 m s-1; time, t = 0.03 s. According to the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so the acceleration, a = (v - u)/t = (0 - 150 m s-1)/0.03 s = -5000 m s-2. (The negative sign indicates that the velocity of the bullet is decreasing.) By the second equation of motion, s = ut + ½at² = (150 m s-1 × 0.03 s) + (½ × (-5000 m s-2) × (0.03 s)²) = 4.50 m - 2.25 m = 2.25 m. By the second law of motion, F = m × a = 0.01 kg × (-5000 m s-2) = -50 N. Hence, the distance of penetration of the bullet into the block is 2.25 m and the magnitude of the force exerted by the wooden block on the bullet is 50 N.

items.stem: An object of mass 1 kg travelling in a straight line with a velocity of 10 m s-1 collides with, and sticks to, a stationary wooden block of mass 5 kg. Then they both move off together in the same straight line. Calculate the total momentum just before the impact and just after the impact. Also, calculate the velocity of the combined object.
items.answer: Given, mass of the object, m1 = 1 kg; initial velocity, u1 = 10 m s-1; mass of the stationary wooden block, m2 = 5 kg; velocity of the wooden block before collision, u2 = 0 m/s. Let the velocity of the combined object be v. Total momentum just before impact = m1 × u1 = 1 kg × 10 m s-1 = 10 kg m s-1. By the law of conservation of momentum, total momentum before impact = total momentum after impact, so the total momentum just after the impact is also 10 kg m s-1. Therefore m1u1 + m2u2 = (m1 + m2)v, that is, 1(10) + 5(0) = (1 + 5)v, so v = 10/6 = 5/3 m s-1 = 1.67 m s-1.
items.concept: Connected objects as a single system

items.stem: An object of mass 100 kg is accelerated uniformly from a velocity of 5 m s-1 to 8 m s-1 in 6 s. Calculate the initial and final momentum of the object. Also, find the magnitude of the force exerted on the object.
items.answer: Given, mass of the object, m = 100 kg; initial velocity, u = 5 m s-1; final velocity, v = 8 m s-1; time, t = 6 s. Initial momentum = m × u = 100 kg × 5 m s-1 = 500 kg m s-1. Final momentum = m × v = 100 kg × 8 m s-1 = 800 kg m s-1. The force is the rate of change of momentum, F = (mv - mu)/t = (800 - 500) kg m s-1 / 6 s = 300 kg m s-1 / 6 s = 50 N.

items.stem: How much momentum will a dumb-bell of mass 10 kg transfer to the floor if it falls from a height of 80 cm? Take its downward acceleration to be 10 m s-2.
items.answer: Given, mass, m = 10 kg; initial velocity, u = 0 m s-1; distance, s = 80 cm = 0.8 m; acceleration, a = 10 m s-2. By the third equation of motion, v² - u² = 2as, so v² - (0 m s-1)² = 2 × 10 m s-2 × 0.8 m, which gives the final velocity, v = 4 m s-1. Momentum transferred to the floor = m × v = 10 kg × 4 m s-1 = 40 kg m s-1.

items.stem: When a force of 40 N is applied on a body it moves with an acceleration of 5 m s-2. Calculate the mass of the body.
items.answer: Let m be the mass of the body. Given, F = 40 N; a = 5 m s-2. From the relation, F = ma, we have 40 = m × 5; hence, m = 40/5 = 8 kg.

items.stem: An object undergoes an acceleration of 8 m s-2 starting from rest. Find the distance travelled in 1 second.
items.answer: Given, acceleration, a = 8 m s-2; initial velocity, u = 0; time interval, t = 1 s; distance travelled, s = ? Using the equation of motion, s = ut + ½at², we get, s = (0 × 1) + (½ × 8 × 1²) = 4 m. The object travels a distance of 4 m.

items.stem: It is required to increase the velocity of a scooter of mass 80 kg from 5 m s-1 to 25 m s-1 in 2 seconds. Calculate the force required.
items.answer: Given, mass of the scooter, m = 80 kg; initial velocity, u = 5 m s-1; final velocity, v = 25 m s-1; time, t = 2 s. Now the acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time, a = (v - u)/t = (25 - 5)/2 = 10 m s-2. Force = mass × acceleration = ma, therefore, F = 80 × 10 = 800 N.

items.stem: Calculate the force required to impart to a car, a velocity of 30 m s-1 in 10 seconds. The mass of the car is 1,500 kg.
items.answer: Given, u = 0 m s-1; v = 30 m s-1; t = 10 s; a = ? Using the relation, v = u + at, we have 30 = 0 + a(10); hence, a = 3 m s-2. Now, F = ma = 1,500 × 3 = 4,500 N.

items.stem: A cricket ball of mass 70 g moving with a velocity of 0.5 m s-1 is stopped by player in 0.5 s. What is the force applied by player to stop the ball?
items.answer: Given, mass of the ball, m = 70 g = 0.070 kg; initial velocity, u = 0.5 m s-1; final velocity, v = 0; time, t = 0.5 s. As we know, F = ma = m[(v - u)/t]. Hence, F = 0.07 × [(0 - 0.50)/0.5] = -0.07 newton. The negative sign indicates that the force exerted by the player is opposite to the direction of motion of the ball.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: What will be acceleration of a body of mass 5 kg if a force of 200 N is applied to it?
items.answer: Given, mass, m = 5 kg; force, F = 200 N. As we know, F = ma, so the acceleration, a = F/m = 200/5 = 40 m s-2.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 10 g is fired from a rifle. The bullet takes 0.003 s to move through its barrel and leaves with a velocity of 300 m s-1. What is the force exerted on the bullet by the rifle?
What force would be needed to produce an acceleration of 1 m s-2 on a ball of mass 1 kg?
items.answer: Given, mass, m = 1 kg; acceleration, a = 1 m s-2. As we know, F = ma = 1 × 1, so, F = 1 newton. One newton is exactly the force that gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.

items.stem: What is the acceleration produced by a force of 5 N exerted on an object of mass 10 kg?
items.answer: Given, F = 5 N; mass, m = 10 kg; acceleration, a = ? As we know, F = ma, or, a = F/m, which gives, a = 0.5 m s-2.

items.stem: How long should a force of 100 N act on a body of 20 kg so that it acquires a velocity of 100 m s-1?
items.answer: Here, v - u = 100 m s-1; m = 20 kg; F = 100 N; t = ? We know that, F = ma = m[(v - u)/t], so, t = [(v - u)/F]m = (100/100) × 20 = 20 s.

items.stem: A 1,000 kg vehicle moving with a speed of 20 m s-1 is brought to rest in a distance of 50 m, (i) Find the acceleration; (ii) Calculate the unbalanced force acting on the vehicle; (iii) The actual force applied by the brakes may be slightly less than that calculated. Why? Give reason.
items.answer: (i) Given, u = 20 m s-1; v = 0; s = 50 m; a = ? Using v² - u² = 2as, we have, a = (v² - u²)/(2s) = (0 - 20²)/(2 × 50) = -400/100 = -4 m s-2. (ii) As we know, F = ma = 1,000 × (-4) = -4,000 N. (iii) Due to the force of friction, the actual force applied by the brakes may be slightly less than the calculated one.
items.concept: Friction brings moving objects to rest

items.stem: Which would require greater force : accelerating a 10 g mass at 5 m s-2 or 20 g mass at 2 m s-2?
items.answer: In the first case, m1 = 10 g = 10/1000 kg = 0.010 kg; a1 = 5 m s-2; F1 = ? So F1 = m1a1 = 0.010 × 5, that is, F1 = 0.050 newton. In the second case, m2 = 20 g = 0.020 kg; a2 = 2 m s-2; F2 = ? So F2 = m2a2 = 0.020 × 2, that is, F2 = 0.04 newton. We find that F1 > F2, hence more force is required to accelerate 10 g at 5 m s-2 than accelerating 20 g at 2 m s-2.

items.stem: A truck starts from rest and rolls down a hill with constant acceleration. It travels a distance of 400 m in 20 s. Find its acceleration. Find the force acting on it if its mass is 7 metric ton.
items.answer: Given, u = 0 m s-1 (starting from rest); s = 400 m; t = 20 s; a = ? Using the relation, s = ut + ½at², we have, 400 = (0 × 20) + (½ × a × 20²) = 200a, so, a = 400/200 = 2 m s-2. Now the mass, m = 7 metric ton = 7,000 kg, so, F = ma = 7,000 × 2 = 14,000 N.

items.stem: A force of 5 N gives a mass m1, an acceleration of 8 m s-2 and a mass m2, an acceleration of 24 m s-2. What acceleration would it give if both the masses are tied together?
items.answer: Let us first find the masses m1 and m2. From the relation, F = m1a1, we get 5 = m1(8), so m1 = 5/8 kg. From the relation, F = m2a2, we get 5 = m2(24), so m2 = 5/24 kg. The total mass, M = m1 + m2 = 5/8 + 5/24 = (15 + 5)/24 = 20/24 kg. Let a be the acceleration produced in the mass M. From the relation, F = Ma, we get 5 = (20/24)a, so, a = 5 × 24/20 = 120/20 = 6 m s-2. Hence, the acceleration of the combination is 6 m s-2.

items.stem: A car of mass 1,000 kg moving with a velocity of 40 km h-1 collides with a tree and comes to stop in 5 s. What will be the force exerted by car on the tree?
items.answer: Given, mass, m = 1,000 kg; initial velocity, u = 40 km h-1 = 100/9 m s-1; final velocity, v = 0; time, t = 5 s. As we know, F = ma = m[(v - u)/t] = 1000 × [(0 - 100/9)/5] = -20000/9 = -2,222 N.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 100 g is fired from a gun of mass 20 kg with a velocity of 100 m s-1. Calculate the velocity of recoil of the gun.
items.answer: Given, mass of the bullet, m = 100 g = 1/10 kg; velocity of the bullet, u = 100 m s-1; mass of the gun, M = 20 kg. Let the recoil velocity of the gun be V. Before firing, the system (gun + bullet) is at rest, therefore the initial momentum of the system = 0. Final momentum of the system = momentum of the bullet + momentum of the gun = mu + MV = (1/10 × 100) + 20V = 10 + 20V. Applying the law of conservation of momentum, final momentum = initial momentum, that is, 10 + 20V = 0, so 20V = -10, or, V = -0.5 m s-1. The negative sign shows that the direction of the recoil velocity of the gun is opposite to the direction of the velocity of the bullet.

items.stem: An iron sphere of mass 10 kg is dropped from a height of 80 cm. If the downward acceleration of the ball is 10 m s-2, calculate the momentum transferred to the ground by the ball.
items.answer: Given, initial velocity of the sphere, u = 0; distance travelled, s = 80 cm = 0.8 m; acceleration of the sphere, a = 10 m s-2. The final velocity of the sphere when it just reaches the ground can be calculated using v² - u² = 2as, so v² - 0 = 2 × 10 × 0.8 = 16, or, v = √16 = 4 m s-1. Momentum of the sphere just before it touches the ground = mv = 10 kg × 4 m s-1 = 40 kg m s-1. On reaching the ground, the iron sphere comes to rest, so its final momentum = 0. According to the law of conservation of momentum, the momentum transferred to the ground = momentum of the sphere just before it comes to rest = 40 kg m s-1.

items.stem: Calculate the force required to impart to a car a velocity of 30 m/s in 10 s. The mass of the car is 1500 kg.
items.answer: Given, u = 0; v = 30 m/s; t = 10 s. As we know, v = u + at, so 30 = 0 + a × 10, which gives, a = 3 m s-2. Now, m = 1500 kg, a = 3 m s-2, so the required force, F = ma = 1500 × 3 = 4500 N.

items.stem: A boy of mass 60 kg running at 3 m/s jumps on to a trolley of mass 140 kg moving with a velocity of 1.5 m/s in the same direction. What is their common velocity?
items.answer: For the boy, m1 = 60 kg, u1 = 3 m s-1, v1 = v. For the trolley, m2 = 140 kg, u2 = 1.5 m s-1, v2 = v. By conservation of momentum, m1u1 + m2u2 = (m1 + m2)v, so (60 × 3) + (140 × 1.5) = (60 + 140)v, that is, v = (180 + 210)/200 = 390/200 = 1.95 m s-1.
items.concept: Connected objects as a single system

items.stem: A bullet of mass 20 g moving with a speed of 500 m s-1 strikes a wooden block of mass 1 kg and gets embedded in it. Find the speed with which block moves along with the bullet.
items.answer: For the bullet, m1 = 20 g = 0.02 kg, u1 = 500 m s-1, v1 = v. For the block, m2 = 1 kg, u2 = 0 m s-1, v2 = v. By conservation of momentum, m1u1 + m2u2 = (m1 + m2)v, so, v = (m1u1 + m2u2)/(m1 + m2) = [(0.02 × 500) + (1 × 0)]/(0.02 + 1) = 10/1.02 = 1000/102 = 9.8 m s-1.
items.concept: Connected objects as a single system

items.stem: A force of 0.6 N acting on a body increases its velocity from 5 m/s to 6 m/s in 2 s. Calculate the mass of the body.
items.answer: Given, F = 0.6 N; u = 5 m s-1; v = 6 m s-1; t = 2 s. The acceleration, a = (v - u)/t = (6 - 5)/2 = ½ = 0.5 m s-2. Hence, the mass, m = F/a = 0.6/0.5 = 1.2 kg.

items.stem: Calculate the force needed to speed up a car with a rate of 5 m s-2, if the mass of the car is 1000 kg.
items.answer: Given, acceleration, a = 5 m/s²; mass, m = 1000 kg; force, F = ? We know that, F = m × a = 1000 kg × 5 m/s² = 5000 kg m/s². Therefore the required force = 5000 kg m/s², or 5000 N.

items.stem: Two persons manage to push a motorcar of mass 1200 kg at a uniform velocity along a level road. The same motorcar can be pushed by three persons to produce an acceleration of 0.2 m s-2. With what force does each person push the motorcar? (Assume that all persons push the motorcar with the same muscular effort)
items.answer: Mass of the motorcar = 1200 kg. Only two persons manage to push the car at a uniform velocity, so the acceleration acquired by the car is given by the third person alone. Acceleration produced in the car when it is pushed by the third person, a = 0.2 m/s². Let the force applied by the third person be F. From Newton’s second law of motion, force = mass × acceleration, so, F = 1200 × 0.2 = 240 N. Thus the third person applies a force of magnitude 240 N. Hence, each person applies a force of 240 N to push the motorcar.

items.stem: A hammer of mass 500 g, moving at 50 m s-1, strikes a nail. The nail stops the hammer in a very short time of 0.01 s. What is the force of the nail on the hammer?
items.answer: Mass of the hammer, m = 500 g = 0.5 kg; initial velocity of the hammer, u = 50 m/s; time taken by the nail to stop the hammer, t = 0.01 s; velocity of the hammer, v = 0 (since the hammer finally comes to rest). From Newton’s second law of motion, the force, F = m[(v - u)/t] = 0.5 × [(0 - 50)/0.01] = -2500 N. The hammer strikes the nail with a force of -2500 N. Hence, from Newton’s third law of motion, the force of the nail on the hammer is equal and opposite, that is, +2500 N.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: A motorcar of mass 1200 kg is moving along a straight line with a uniform velocity of 90 km/h. Its velocity is slowed down to 18 km/h in 4 s by an unbalanced external force. Calculate the acceleration and change in momentum. Also calculate the magnitude of the force required.
items.answer: Mass of the motorcar, m = 1200 kg; initial velocity of the motorcar, u = 90 km/h = 25 m/s; final velocity of the motorcar, v = 18 km/h = 5 m/s; time taken, t = 4 s.
